prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Alibaba Group Holding Ltd" (ticker BABA), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BABA", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Alibaba Group Holding Limited
markets: Quick commerce and food delivery (Taobao Instant Commerce, Ele.me)
Cloud computing and AI models (Alibaba Cloud, Qwen)
Cross-border and international e-commerce (AliExpress, Lazada, Trendyol, Alibaba.com)
Digital media, maps and other services (Youku, Amap, DingTalk, Freshippo)

mission.statement: To make it easy to do business anywhere.
mission.source: Alibaba Group website and annual report (Form 20-F)
mission.plain: Alibaba wants to help any business, big or small, sell and grow anywhere using its technology.

about.plain: Alibaba runs China's biggest online shopping sites, Taobao and Tmall, where millions of shops sell to Chinese shoppers. It makes most of its money by charging those shops for ads and services. It also rents out computers and AI over the internet through Alibaba Cloud and builds its own AI models called Qwen. It runs shopping sites in other countries too, like AliExpress and Lazada.
about.customers: Chinese shoppers and the millions of merchants and brands that pay to sell and advertise to them, plus businesses that use its cloud and AI.
about.everyday: If you have ordered cheap goods on AliExpress or heard of Singles' Day shopping, that is Alibaba.

money.plain: ads and fees paid by merchants, plus direct sales
renting computers, storage and AI models to companies
food and goods delivered within an hour
AI chatbots, models and AI chips (T-Head)
Cainiao logistics, Freshippo stores, Amap, Youku, DingTalk

result.summary: Alibaba still has a real but narrower moat: Taobao and Tmall remain China's largest marketplaces with strong network effects and merchant ad spending, and Alibaba Cloud is China's leading cloud and AI provider with about 36% share. Its retail advantage has been eroded by PDD, Douyin and JD, regulators limit its power, and heavy spending on quick commerce and AI has cut operating profit sharply.

pricingPower.evidence: In September 2024 Alibaba introduced a 0.6% basic software service fee on Taobao and Tmall merchant sales and lifted customer management revenue without losing merchant share, but fierce competition from PDD, JD and Douyin forces heavy subsidies, and China e-commerce revenue fell 8% in the June 2026 quarter.

moats.evidence: Taobao, Tmall and Singles' Day (11.11) are among China's best-known consumer brands, and Tmall is the default flagship-store channel for global brands in China.
Alibaba Cloud enterprise customers and the 50-million-plus 88VIP members face some switching costs, but Chinese shoppers and merchants multi-home easily across PDD, JD and Douyin.
Taobao and Tmall connect hundreds of millions of shoppers with millions of merchants, and the scale of buyers keeps merchants paying for advertising on the platforms.

With FY2026 revenue of about RMB1.02 trillion and China's largest cloud footprint, Alibaba has data-centre and purchasing scale, but it is spending a RMB380 billion-plus three-year AI infrastructure budget to keep up.
China e-commerce supports several large profitable players (PDD, JD, Douyin, Kuaishou), so Alibaba's market is not a natural monopoly.
Alibaba has been on the receiving end of counter-positioning, as PDD's low-price, group-buying model and Douyin's content-led shopping took share it struggled to defend.
Alibaba handles Singles' Day peak transaction loads with in-house infrastructure and has built leading open-source AI models (Qwen family), know-how that is hard to replicate.
Its T-Head chip unit and AI talent are valuable but not exclusive, and US export controls limit its access to the most advanced Nvidia GPUs.

customers.evidence: 88VIP paying membership passed 50 million and Taobao app usage recovered after 2024, but many Chinese shoppers now compare prices across PDD, JD and Douyin, and merchants complain about fees and forced discounting.

talent.evidence: Alibaba remains one of China's most sought-after tech employers and its Qwen team is highly regarded, but the 2020-2023 regulatory crackdown, restructurings and layoffs, and poaching by ByteDance and AI start-ups have weakened its pull.

product.evidence: Qwen models rank among the top open-weight AI models in public benchmarks and Alibaba Cloud leads China cloud with about 36% share (Omdia, Q3 2025), but its shopping apps are no longer clearly best in class versus PDD on price or JD on delivery.

threats: Continued share loss in China e-commerce to PDD, Douyin and JD (China E-commerce revenue fell 8% in the June 2026 quarter)
A costly quick-commerce subsidy war with Meituan and JD that drove operating income down 64% in FY2026
AI capex (RMB67.7B in the June 2026 quarter, up 75%) pushing free cash flow deeply negative before AI returns are proven
US export controls limiting access to advanced AI chips, and US delisting or investment-restriction risk for Chinese ADRs
Chinese regulatory intervention, as in the 2021 RMB18.2B antitrust fine and the halted Ant Group IPO
Weak Chinese consumer spending and deflationary pricing pressure

ceo.name: Eddie Wu (Wu Yongming)
ceo.background: One of Alibaba's 18 co-founders; engineering graduate of Zhejiang University of Technology; former Alipay CTO and Taobao executive; also leads Alibaba Cloud

c1.evidence: Alibaba Cloud leads China's fast-growing cloud and AI market (about 36% share, cloud revenue up 45% in the June 2026 quarter), but its core e-commerce market is mature and contested.

c2.evidence: Shoppers and brands choose Tmall for authentic branded goods and Taobao for selection, but PDD's prices and JD's delivery have shown that advantage can be copied.

c3.evidence: Alibaba is a household name in China and widely known abroad, but it is no longer the undisputed default for Chinese online shopping.

c4.evidence: 'Make it easy to do business anywhere' still guides the company and Eddie Wu has reframed it around AI, but the past decade was dominated by regulatory retreat and restructuring.

c6.evidence: “Jack Ma, Taobao, Singles' Day, cheap AliExpress goods” - impressions are mostly positive in China but mixed abroad because of counterfeit concerns and China-related regulatory and geopolitical risk.

c7.evidence: It rides the secular growth of AI and cloud in China, where Alibaba plans to spend over RMB380 billion on AI and cloud infrastructure over three years.

c8.evidence: Alibaba is expanding into AI models and apps (Qwen), AI chips (T-Head), quick commerce and international markets such as Turkey (Trendyol) and Southeast Asia (Lazada).

m1.evidence: Eddie Wu has set out a clear 'user first, AI-driven' strategy and talks about artificial superintelligence as the goal of Alibaba's AI investment.

m2.evidence: Wu is one of the 18 co-founders who started Alibaba in Jack Ma's apartment in 1999 and has refocused the company on long-term AI bets despite near-term profit pressure.

m4.evidence: Wu has pushed a 'user first' turnaround for Taobao, but staff have faced restructurings and layoffs and merchants have complained about fees.

m5.evidence: Under Wu, Alibaba has produced the widely used Qwen open-source model family and new AI products, though the culture was weakened by the 2021-2023 crackdown and break-up plans.

m6.evidence: Wu has a technical background as Alipay's former CTO and personally runs Alibaba Cloud as well as the group.

m7.evidence: Wu keeps a low public profile and there is little public evidence either way about his personal character beyond his long service to the company.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Eddie Wu at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university has been found.

m8b.evidence: Wu is reserved and engineering-minded, unlike Alibaba's flamboyant co-founder Jack Ma.

m9.evidence: Since 2023 he reaccelerated cloud growth to 45% and returned China e-commerce to growth in FY2026, but operating income fell 64% in FY2026 and 57% in the June 2026 quarter.

m10.evidence: Alibaba has sold non-core assets such as Sun Art and Intime and cut costs, yet it is now spending heavily on subsidies and AI.

c10.evidence: Taobao and Tmall serve hundreds of millions of Chinese consumers and millions of small merchants, and Qwen is among the most downloaded open-source AI model families.

p2.evidence: Running a cloud and frontier AI models is very hard and important, while marketplaces are easier to copy, as PDD showed.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from RMB717B in FY2021 to RMB1,024B in FY2026, though growth slowed to 2-8% in recent years.

f2.evidence: Operating margin fell from about 12.5% in FY2021 to about 4.9% in FY2026, and gross margin is roughly flat to down (about 39.8% in FY2026).

f3.evidence: At 30 June 2026 Alibaba held RMB474.5B of cash and liquid investments versus about RMB266.5B of borrowings and notes, with large positive equity, though free cash flow is now negative.

f4.evidence: Operating income fell from about RMB90B in FY2021 to RMB50B in FY2026 and operating cash flow from over RMB230B to RMB76B.

v1.evidence: Shoppers now have strong alternatives such as PDD for the lowest prices and JD for fast, reliable delivery, so Alibaba is not clearly the best choice.

v2.evidence: Alibaba has appeared on Chinese best-employer lists and remains a prized employer for tech graduates, but no recent global ranking puts it among the very best places to work.

c5.evidence: If Alibaba disappeared, millions of Chinese merchants would lose their main online store and ad channel, and many Chinese companies running on Alibaba Cloud and Qwen would be disrupted.
